cards.front: In the strawberry DNA activity, what is in the white, stringy clump that collects under the alcohol?
cards.back: Many DNA molecules plus some other cell material. It is not pure DNA.
cards.quote: The clump holds many DNA molecules plus some other cell material.

cards.front: Why can the white clump from the strawberry activity show you DNA but not tell you how much DNA the strawberry has?
cards.back: The clump is not pure DNA, so it shows that DNA is there but does not measure an amount.
cards.quote: It shows you DNA, but it is not pure and does not measure an amount.

cards.front: What are the two sides of the DNA ladder made of, and what makes up the rungs?
cards.back: The sides are sugar and phosphate. The rungs are pairs of the bases A, T, C and G.
cards.why: The order of the bases is the code.
cards.quote: Key idea: DNA is a double helix whose sugar-phosphate sides are the same in all living things, while the order of the bases in the rungs is the code.

cards.front: Why is the sugar-phosphate side of DNA not where the code is?
cards.back: The sides are the same in all living things, so they carry no differences. The order of the bases in the rungs is the code.
cards.quote: Key idea: DNA is a double helix whose sugar-phosphate sides are the same in all living things, while the order of the bases in the rungs is the code.

cards.front: In ordinary double-stranded DNA, A pairs with {{c1::T}}, and C pairs with G.
cards.quote: In ordinary double-stranded DNA, A pairs with T, and C pairs with G.

cards.front: One side of a piece of DNA reads G A C T T. What does the partner side read?
cards.back: C T G A A. Pair each position separately: G with C, A with T, C with G, T with A, and T with A.
cards.quote: Pair each position separately: G with C, A with T, C with G, T with A, and T with A.

cards.front: One side of a piece of DNA reads A A C G T T. How many T bases does the partner side have?
cards.back: Two. The partner reads T T G C A A, because A pairs with T, C with G, G with C and T with A. Each A on the first side puts a T on the other.
cards.quote: In ordinary double-stranded DNA, A pairs with T, and C pairs with G.

cards.front: Why can scientists write a stretch of DNA as just letters, such as ATTGCAC?
cards.back: They skip the sides, because the sides never change. Only the order of the bases differs.
cards.quote: They skip the sides, because the sides never change.

cards.front: DNA is a bit like letters in a word. What happens to the message if you rearrange the bases?
cards.back: The message can change, just as rearranged letters can change a word. The order of the bases matters.
cards.why: A cell does not read words; its molecules follow the bases in order.
cards.quote: DNA is a bit like letters in a word. If you rearrange the letters, the message can change.

cards.front: A {{c1::chromosome}} is a long strand of DNA packaged with proteins.
cards.quote: A chromosome is a long strand of DNA packaged with proteins.
cards.section: Add scale and limits to the gene model

cards.front: A {{c1::gene}} is a section of a chromosome, and one chromosome carries many genes.
cards.quote: A gene is a section of a chromosome, and one chromosome carries many genes.
cards.section: Add scale and limits to the gene model

cards.front: In plants, animals and fungi, where does most DNA sit in the cell?
cards.back: In the nucleus. Fungi such as mushrooms have DNA too, not only animals.
cards.quote: In plants, animals and fungi, most DNA sits in the nucleus, which you met in Inside a Cell.
cards.section: Add scale and limits to the gene model

cards.front: Before a cell divides, its chromosomes pack down even further. Does tighter packing make them easier or harder to see with a microscope?
cards.back: Easier. Packed chromosomes become thick enough to see with a microscope.
cards.quote: Before a cell divides, its chromosomes pack down even further.
cards.section: Add scale and limits to the gene model

cards.front: What do proteins do in cells? Give two examples.
cards.back: Proteins build cells, tissues and organs and do most of the work in cells. Some form hair, some carry oxygen in blood, and some speed up reactions.
cards.quote: Some form hair, some carry oxygen in blood, and some speed up reactions.
cards.section: Add scale and limits to the gene model

cards.front: How do the order of bases in DNA, proteins and traits connect?
cards.back: Many genes carry base sequences used to build proteins, and proteins can affect traits. So the base order can shape traits.
cards.quote: Key idea: Many genes carry base sequences used to build proteins, and proteins can affect traits.
cards.section: Add scale and limits to the gene model

cards.front: A skin cell and a muscle cell from the same person look very different. Which explanation fits best: different DNA, or the same DNA with different genes in use?
cards.back: The same DNA, with different genes in use. Different genes make different proteins, and proteins shape what a cell looks like and does.
cards.why: Gene use, not a different DNA set, is what differs.
cards.quote: Sequence works through genes, proteins and gene use; many traits also depend on several genes and the surroundings.

cards.front: In the pea plant model, you change one base and press Read the gene. What do you expect to see, and where does the model differ from real cells?
cards.back: The model links one base change to one protein change and one trait change, so you can test a cause. Real cells are messier: some base changes alter nothing you can see.
cards.quote: Real cells are messier: some base changes alter nothing you can see.
cards.section: Test the code in a model

cards.front: One onion set has about 16,400 million base pairs. One human set has 3,055 million. About how many times as much DNA does the onion set have?
cards.back: Divide 16,400 by 3,055, which is about 5.4. The onion set has about 5 times as much DNA as the human set.
cards.quote: Divide the onion amount by the human amount.
cards.section: Work with the full DNA-amount data

cards.front: Put these in order from least DNA to most: onion, human, E. coli, rice, baker's yeast, fruit fly, thale cress, woodland strawberry.
cards.back: E. coli (4.6), baker's yeast (12.1), thale cress (about 157), fruit fly (about 175), woodland strawberry (about 240), rice (about 389), human (3,055), onion (about 16,400), all in millions of base pairs per set.
cards.quote: List the eight living things from least DNA to most.
cards.section: Work with the full DNA-amount data

cards.front: A classmate says living things with more DNA are more complex. Use the table of DNA amounts to answer with a claim, evidence and reasoning.
cards.back: Claim: DNA amount does not rank complexity. Evidence: an onion has about 16,400 million base pairs, about 5 times a human's 3,055 million. Reasoning: if more DNA meant more complex, the onion would outrank the human.
cards.quote: base order carries instructions, but the total amount of DNA is not a complexity score.

cards.front: Plan a fair test of whether more dish soap gives a bigger clump in the strawberry activity. Name the variables, control and trials.
cards.back: Independent variable: 0, 5 and 10 mL of soap. Dependent variable: mass of the wet clump in grams. Constants: 50 g of strawberry, salt, water, mashing time, filter and amount of cold alcohol. Control: the 0 mL cup. Three cups per amount, then find each mean.
cards.quote: Independent variable: dish soap in the mix: 0 mL, 5 mL and 10 mL.

cards.front: In the soap test, the clump grows as soap goes up. What can you conclude, and what can you not?
cards.back: It fits the idea that soap opens more cells, but it does not prove it. The clump is not pure DNA, so its mass is only a rough measure.
cards.quote: If the clump grows as soap goes up, that fits the idea that soap opens more cells. It does not prove it.
